title: Location Data Collection
description: Your company is storing precise user location data unnecessarily. Your manager, a 'Diluter,' consistently minimizes the problem's importance using statistics, resource constraints, and ROI arguments to avoid a fix.
initial_user_message: Hi, I've been reviewing our location data collection practices, and we're storing precise GPS coordinates for features that only need general city-level information. This seems like an unnecessary privacy risk for our users that we should address.

step_1.text: Thanks for flagging this. I've looked at the data, and let's keep it in perspective. The number of users who have actually complained about our privacy settings is less than 0.1%. And compared to other apps in our space, we're already collecting less data. Most users seem totally fine with our current approach.

user_choices.choice: Even if no one complains, it's our responsibility to protect user privacy by default. They trust us with their data.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You immediately rejected the 'lack of complaints' argument and refocused on the core principle of trust and responsibility.

user_choices.choice: You're right, if users aren't complaining, it's probably not a high-priority issue for them.
user_choices.justification: You've accepted the manager's flawed logic that a lack of complaints means there is no problem.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable using 'better than other apps' as our standard. We should be setting the standard for user privacy.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the comparative argument and appealing to a higher, internal standard.

user_choices.choice: If most users are fine with it, then I guess our current approach is working.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that accepts the manager's premise without questioning if 'most users' is the right metric.

step_2.text: I appreciate the principle, but we have to be practical about where we spend our time. We have two weeks before the next release. This privacy change would probably take a week of engineering. Meanwhile, we have a performance bug that's slowing down the app for 15% of all users. We have to prioritize the work that helps the most people, right?

user_choices.choice: What if we did a quick, one-day fix? Just changing the data type we store is a small change that has a huge privacy impact.
user_choices.justification: A great move. You've countered the resource argument by proposing a smaller, more achievable scope.

user_choices.choice: You're right, fixing a bug for 15% of users does seem like a higher priority than a privacy issue for a smaller group.
user_choices.justification: You've accepted the manager's utilitarian math, agreeing to sacrifice the privacy of a minority group.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'enhancement' we can de-prioritize; it's a fundamental privacy risk. That should be as important as a performance bug.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're correctly framing privacy as a core requirement, not an optional feature.

user_choices.choice: I suppose if it's a choice between helping many users or a few, we have to choose the many.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's false choice, ignoring the possibility that both issues could be addressed.

user_choices.choice: You're right, from a pure cost-benefit perspective, the numbers are hard to justify.

bad_ending.text: The manager successfully uses statistics and comparisons to avoid addressing privacy issues. Location data collection continues unchanged, with users unaware of the unnecessary precision being captured and the privacy implications downplayed through selective metrics.
bad_ending.title: Statistical Minimization Success
bad_ending.learning: Diluter managers use statistics and benchmarks to make privacy issues seem insignificant. Focusing on user rights rather than percentages helps maintain momentum for privacy improvements regardless of complaint volumes.

mid_ending.text: Some minor privacy improvements are implemented, but the manager successfully uses resource scarcity and statistical arguments to limit comprehensive privacy protection. Metrics and comparisons prevent substantive changes to data collection practices.
mid_ending.title: Numbers Game Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial progress with diluter managers often comes with statistical justifications for inadequate privacy protection. Demonstrating user value beyond metrics helps counter arguments about resource priorities.

good_ending.text: Despite the manager's statistical minimization and resource arguments, meaningful privacy improvements are implemented. User location data collection is reduced to necessary levels regardless of complaint percentages or industry comparisons.
good_ending.title: User Rights Over Statistics
good_ending.learning: Success against diluter managers requires focusing on user rights and values rather than engaging with statistical minimization. Privacy protection shouldn't depend on complaint volumes or industry benchmarks.
